I. There is no mention of it in the Constitution.

II. A period of six months must lapse between the introduction of one ‘No Confidence Motion’ and another.

III. At least 100 persons must support such a motion before it is introduced in the House.

IV. It can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only.
Codes
x: The no-confidence motion is not mentioned in the Constitution (it flows from Art 75(3)) and can be moved in the Lok Sabha only. The support needed is 50 members, not 100, and there is no six-month gap rule, so II and III are wrong.

s: Vote of no-confidence motion is brought in which house?
x: A no-confidence motion is moved only in the Lok Sabha because the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to that House.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding a No-Confidence Motion in India.

I. There is no mention of a No-Confidence Motion in the Constitution of India.

II. A motion of No-Confidence can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Constitution does not mention a no-confidence motion; it flows from Art 75(3). It can be moved in the Lok Sabha only, so both statements are correct.

s: What minimum support is needed for leave to move a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha?
x: It needs 50 members' support; the motion is not expressly in the Constitution but flows from Article 75(3) and lies only in the Lok Sabha.

s: Who moved the first no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers, against Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963?
x: The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by J.B. Kripalani.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A Censure Motion may be directed against a Minister, a group of Ministers or the whole Council.
A No-confidence Motion is directed against the entire Council of Ministers.
Passing a Censure Motion compels the Council of Ministers to resign.
Passing a No-confidence Motion requires the Council of Ministers to resign.
x: A passed Censure Motion does not compel resignation; a passed No-confidence Motion does.

s: What happens if a Confidence Motion moved by the Government is defeated in the Lok Sabha?
o: The Lok Sabha is automatically dissolved
The motion is referred to the Committee of Privileges
x: Defeat of a confidence motion shows the Government has lost the Lok Sabha's support, so it falls.

s: Who moves a Confidence Motion in the Lok Sabha?
x: The Government moves a confidence motion to prove its majority; a no-confidence motion is moved by the Opposition.

s: Which of the following pairs about a no-confidence motion is correctly matched?
o: House where moved – Lok Sabha only
Rule of the Lok Sabha – Rule 184
x: A no-confidence motion (Rule 198) is moved only in the Lok Sabha with 50 members' support and needs no reasons.

s: Which motion must state specific reasons for its adoption?
x: A censure motion must state reasons; a no-confidence motion needs 50 members' support but no reasons, and the government moves a confidence motion.

s: Who moved the no-confidence motion carried against the Prakasam ministry of Andhra State in November 1954?
x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion was carried by 69 votes to 68 in November 1954, and the Prakasam ministry fell.

s: Who decides whether a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha is admitted?
x: The Speaker has discretion to admit or reject a no-confidence motion; reasons need not be stated.

s: By what margin was the no-confidence motion against the Prakasam ministry of Andhra State (1954) carried?
x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion passed 69–68 and the Prakasam ministry fell by one vote after 13 months.

s: Against whom is a no-confidence motion directed?
x: A no-confidence motion is against the whole Council of Ministers; if passed, the whole CoM must resign.

s: To whom is notice of a no-confidence motion given in writing?
x: Written notice goes to the Secretary-General, and at least 50 members must support leave to move it.

s: By what majority must a resolution to remove the Lok Sabha Speaker under Article 94(c) be passed?
o: A majority of all the then members of the House
A simple majority of members present and voting
Two-thirds of members present and voting
x: Removal needs a majority of all the then members (an effective majority), after 14 days' notice; a simple majority is not enough.

s: What happens if a censure motion against a minister is passed?
x: A censure motion expresses disapproval of policy; unlike a no-confidence motion, it does not force resignation.

s: When was President's Rule imposed in Andhra State after the Prakasam ministry fell by one vote?
x: After Gouthu Latchanna's no-confidence motion passed 69-68, President's Rule ran from 16 November 1954 to 27 March 1955.

s: Which of the following proposals is related to the Union Budget?
x: Censure Motion: Censure means the expression of strong disapproval or harsh criticism. It is generally against the policies of the Government. Calling Attention : With the prior permission of the Speaker, a member may call the attention of a Minister to any matter of urgent public importance and the Minister may make a brief statement or ask for time to make a statement at a later hour or date. Cut Motion : Cut motion is a power given to a member of the Lok Sabha to oppose a demand in the Financial Bill discussed by the Government. If a cut motion is adopted by the House and the Government does not have the numbers, it is obliged to resign. However the Lok Sabha has the right to permit the grant after reducing the amount, and they do so by a cut motion which are of three types-token cut, policy cut, and frugality cut. Adjournment Motion: It is a motion to draw the attention of members of the House to a subject or matter of public importance.

s: A motion moved by Member of Parliament when he feels a minster has committed a breach of privilege of the House with holding facts of a case is called
x: A privilege motion is moved against a Minister who withholds or distorts facts. It is referred to the Committee of Privileges, unlike a censure or no-confidence motion.

s: Which of the following statements about a Privilege Motion is incorrect?
o: It automatically forces the Government to resign.
It may be raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts.
It requires the consent of the Presiding Officer.
It is admissible in either House of Parliament.

s: Which of the following pairs of cut motions is correctly matched?

s: By how much does a token cut motion reduce a demand for grant?
x: A token cut reduces the demand by Rs 100 to air a specific grievance; a policy cut reduces it to Re 1.

s: In which House can a privilege motion against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts be moved?
x: A privilege motion can be moved in either House with the presiding officer's consent and does not force resignation.

s:
Which of the following statement/statements is/are valid regarding the office of the 'Whip'?

I. Although not mentioned in the Constitution of India, the office of the 'Whip' has however been incorporated in the Rules of the House by the 'Leaders and Chief Whips of Recognised Parties and Groups in Parliament (Facilities) Act, 1998'.

II. The role of the Chief Whip of the government party in the Lok Sabha is served by the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs.

III. All political parties – whether ruling or opposition, will have their own Whips in the Parliament.

IV. The Chief Whip is not responsible to the leader of the House but is responsible only to the leader of the party that has appointed him/her to the office of Chief Whip.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
x: Only statement III is valid: the 1998 Act merely gives Chief Whips facilities rather than incorporating the office into House rules, and the Lok Sabha Government Chief Whip is the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs (the Minister of State holds the post in the Rajya Sabha), so only III is correct.

s: From what does the office of Whip in the Indian parliamentary system primarily derive its authority?
o: The Rules of Procedure of Parliament
A specific provision of the Constitution
x: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any parliamentary statute. It is based on conventions of parliamentary government.

s: On which days are Private Members' Resolutions in Parliament generally taken up?

x: Private Members’ Resolutions are taken up on alternate Fridays during the afternoon.

s: What is a resolution moved under a constitutional or statutory provision called?
x: Such a resolution is a statutory resolution; a Government resolution is one moved by a minister, e.g. to approve a treaty.

s: For how long is a resolution on the same subject barred after a resolution has been moved in Parliament?
x: A resolution on the same subject is barred for one year; a resolution is always a substantive motion, must be put to vote, and cannot be withdrawn without the House's leave.

s: Which Union Minister maintains close contact with the Chief Whips of political parties in both Houses of Parliament?

x: The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs keeps close contact with the Chief Whips of parties in both Houses.

s: Under which Schedule can defiance of a party Whip attract disqualification?
x: The Whip enforces attendance and voting on party lines, and defiance can attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Two-line Whip – Direction to attend the House
One-line Whip – Direction to attend the House
x: A two-line Whip directs members to attend; a one-line Whip is informative and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.

s: With what can the mover withdraw a resolution moved in Parliament?
o: Consent of the Business Advisory Committee
x: A resolution is a substantive motion that must be put to vote; the mover cannot withdraw it without leave of the House.

s: What does a three-line whip direct members to do?
o: Vote strictly as the party directs
x: A one-line whip informs, a two-line whip directs attendance and a three-line whip is a strict voting direction.

s: From which session was biometric attendance for MLAs introduced in the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
x: Andhra Pradesh introduced biometric attendance for MLAs from its Budget Session in 2026.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

s: Which is largest committee of the Indian Parliament?
x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, which makes it the largest committee. PAC and COPU have 22 each, and the Petitions Committee has 25 (LS 15, RS 10).

s: The reason for the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament being headed by a member of the opposition party in the Lok Sabha is
x: The Public Accounts Committee is headed by an opposition member of the Lok Sabha by convention, not by a statutory rule.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Public Accounts Committee?
o: A Minister can be a member of the Committee.
It has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
Its members are elected annually by PR-STV.
Its Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
x: Ministers cannot be members of the Public Accounts Committee.

s: On whose recommendation was the Committee on Public Undertakings (1964) created?

s: In which year was the Public Accounts Committee first set up?

s: Which committee is described as the “Continuous economy committee”?
x: The Estimates Committee is known as the “Continuous economy committee.”

s: Which parliamentary committee has 30 members drawn from the Lok Sabha only and is the largest parliamentary committee?
x: The Estimates Committee is the largest parliamentary committee, with 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha. The PAC and Public Undertakings Committee have 22 members each.

s: Since 1967, the Chairman of which committee has been appointed from the Opposition?
x: The Speaker has appointed the PAC Chairman from the Opposition since 1967; the Estimates Committee Chairman comes from the ruling party.

s: For what term are members of the three Financial Committees of Parliament elected?
x: Members of the PAC, Estimates and Public Undertakings Committees are elected by PR-STV for one year.

s: What is the status of the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee?
o: binding once approved by the Speaker
x: PAC recommendations are not binding; the PAC checks spending within the scope of the demand and examines execution, not policy.

s: How many members does the Public Accounts Committee have?
x: The PAC has 22 members, 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha; 30 from the Lok Sabha only is the Estimates Committee.

s: On whose recommendation did the Estimates Committee take its present form in 1950?
x: The Estimates Committee dates from 1921 and took its present form in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation; Krishna Menon is linked to COPU.

s: Who headed the Public Accounts Committee of the 18th Lok Sabha?

s: Which of the following is NOT a financial committee of Parliament?

s: To which House does the Public Accounts Committee submit its report?

Neither House; it reports to the CAG
x: The PAC reports to the Lok Sabha through the Speaker; a copy is laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.

s: How many members does the Committee on Public Undertakings have?
x: Like the PAC, the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.

s: From which party is the Chairman of the Estimates Committee usually appointed?
o: Any party in the Rajya Sabha
x: The Estimates Committee chair comes from the ruling party, whereas the PAC chair has come from the Opposition since 1967.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes of the Parliament of India:

s:
Consider the following statements in respect of questions asked by the Members in the Parliament of India:
1. Unstarred questions are those to which a Member desires an oral answer in the House.
2. Starred questions are those to which a Member desires a written answer.
3. No supplementary question can be asked on an unstarred question. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct?
o: All the three statements are correct.
There are two correct statements, that include statement 2.
There is only one correct statement.
x: Statement 1 is incorrect: Unstarred Questions require a written answer, not an oral answer. A Starred Question is the one that requires an oral answer. Statement 2 is incorrect: Starred Questions require an oral answer, not a written one. Statement 3 is correct: Since Unstarred Questions are answered in writing, no supplementary question can be asked on them.
